chunk_findings.detail:
Registration is decided by a **text** match, not by importing the module and checking the attribute: `_HAS_COMMANDS.search(path.read_text("utf-8"))` with `RE.MULTILINE` matches `COMMANDS` at the start of *any* line, including lines inside a docstring or multi-line string literal. A helper sitting next to the families, e.g.

```python
"""Shared parameter helpers.

COMMANDS that use these params build them here.
"""
```

matches, so `family_modules()` imports it, and then `all_commands()` executes `m.COMMANDS` for a module that has no `COMMANDS` attribute → `AttributeError: module 'ddflow.surfaces.declared.mutation_params' has no attribute 'COMMANDS'`. Because `all_commands()` is evaluated at import time in `exemptions.py` (`*all_commands()` inside the `DECLARATIONS` tuple), the crash is at package import, not at first command use, and it takes down every surface that imports `ddflow.surfaces.exemptions`. The declared docstring explicitly claims helper modules are "never imported by the scan" — the guarantee only holds for helpers that happen to contain no line beginning with `COMMANDS`, so the invariant is text-dependent rather than structural. Importing the candidate (or checking `hasattr`/`getattr(m, "COMMANDS", None)`) instead of grepping source removes the whole class of false positives.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py:21 (`family_modules` / `_HAS_COMMANDS`)

chunk_findings.detail: `all_commands()` returns families in file-name order, which is not the order the tuple previously encoded, so the registry consumed downstream is reordered. The old curated order had `_RECORDS` before `_RECORDKINDS` and `_REPORTING` before `_REPORT`; the alphabetical scan yields `records`/`recordkinds` → `recordkinds` before `records`, and `report` before `reporting` (and `report` before `reporting` also moves relative to `review`/`rules`). Any consumer that resolves a tool/command name by scanning `DECLARATIONS` in order and keeping the first (or last) match — the kind of lookup the neighbouring `covering_tools` implies — now attributes an overlapping name to a different declaration than it did before this change, changing which exemption/coverage applies to that tool; order-based help grouping is affected the same way. If order is genuinely no longer meaningful this needs to be stated and enforced (e.g. sorted explicitly inside the consumer), otherwise the curated ordering must be preserved rather than replaced by filesystem order.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/exemptions.py:62 (`DECLARATIONS = (*EXEMPTIONS, *all_commands(), ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The change adds `help_group` to the MCP tool entry:

    if self.help_group:
        entry["help_group"] = self.help_group

but the same hunk rewrites `Command`'s contract to say the opposite: "`tool_entry` carries neither tier nor group: the engine reads tiers from the tier table, not from the entry." So the code and the stated contract it was just given disagree: for any `Command` with `help_group="…"` (exactly the value the new field exists to hold), `tool_entry()` now returns a dict containing `help_group`, which the docstring asserts it does not carry. Because `tool_entry` is the MCP tool descriptor, this is not merely stale prose: it changes the key set/wire shape of the tool listing that `tests/test_api_layer.py`'s wire-shape rows and any consumer of the MCP tool descriptor observe. Either the entry must not carry `help_group` (and `services/help.py` should read it off the `Command` as the docstring describes), or the documented contract that "the entry carries neither tier nor group" has to be dropped — as written, one of the two is wrong for every tool that declares a help group.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py (`Command.tool_entry`, the added `entry["help_group"]`

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten guard advertises a check it cannot perform. `ORDER` is built as `*LEGACY_ORDER` followed by the declared/hand-written names not already in `LEGACY_ORDER`, and `TOOLS` is then materialised with `DECLARED[name].tool_entry() if name in DECLARED else HAND_WRITTEN[name] for name in ORDER`. Any name in `LEGACY_ORDER` that is in neither `DECLARED` nor `HAND_WRITTEN` is dereferenced by that comprehension *before* the `raise` runs, so it raises a bare `KeyError` from the dict literal instead of reaching `RuntimeError("tools/order.py lists a tool twice, or names one nothing declares")` — the exact scenario the new message claims to diagnose. Concrete input: `tools/order.py` still lists a tool that a migration moved out of `HAND_WRITTEN` (or whose `declared/<family>.py` file was renamed), leaving `LEGACY_ORDER` a name nothing declares; the module fails at import with `KeyError: '<name>'` and the intended diagnostic is dead code. The condition should be checked (or the lookup made tolerant) before `TOOLS` is built.

chunk_findings.detail: The new comprehension reads `(tools[t] or {}).get("help_group")`. The `isinstance(tools, Mapping)` guard only checks the container type, never the value type, so any mapping whose values are not dict-like raises `AttributeError` on every help render. Before this change the values were never touched — `tools = list(tools)` simply took the keys — so a name-keyed registry such as `{"ddflow status": "show the queue", "ddflow claim": "claim the next item"}` (name → description string), or the name → `Command` shape the intent describes ("help group read from the Command itself", which would need `getattr`, not `.get`), used to render fine and now crashes with `'str' object has no attribute 'get'` / `'Command' object has no attribute 'get'`. Either guard the values (`isinstance(tools[t], Mapping)`) or read the attribute off the object that actually carries `help_group`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_HAS_COMMANDS = re.compile(r"^COMMANDS\s*(?::[^=\n]+)?=", re.MULTILINE)` only recognizes a *single-line* declaration: the optional annotation group is `[^=\n]+`, so any family whose annotation wraps is not imported at all. Concretely, a new one-file family written as

```python
COMMANDS: tuple[
    Command,
    ...,
] = (
    ...
)
```

fails the regex (after `COMMANDS:` the group can't cross the newline, the group is skipped, and `=` no longer follows), so `family_modules()` never imports the module and `all_commands()` silently omits all of its commands from `DECLARATIONS` in exemptions.py — the CLI commands simply do not exist, with no error, which defeats the "adding a command is one new file" contract (any formatting other than a one-line annotation silently unregisters the family). The same textual detector also over-matches: a helper module with a triple-quoted string containing a column-0 `COMMANDS = (` line is imported and then raises `AttributeError` on `m.COMMANDS`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py `_HAS_COMMANDS` (family_modules)

chunk_findings.detail: The MCP-table filter is purely textual and requires a literal double-quoted prefix: `_HAS_TOOL = re.compile(r'\btool\s*=\s*"ddflow_')`. A family that declares `tool='ddflow_x'` (single quotes), `tool=f"ddflow_{name}"`, or `tool=TOOL_X` where the name is a module constant, matches `_HAS_COMMANDS` but not `_HAS_TOOL`. In that case `all_commands(tools=True)` skips it, so the command keeps working on the CLI but is silently missing from the MCP tool table — a registration regression that produces no error and is only visible at call time. Because the filter decides correctness from source text rather than from the `Command` object itself, the two detectors can disagree about which families exist.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py `_HAS_TOOL` (family_modules)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff changes `Tool.tier` from a working default (`"standard"`) to an empty-string sentinel and documents `""` as a "registration error", but nothing in the changed code enforces that. `tier` is not emitted by `tool_entry` either, so the only consumer is `tools/tiers.py`, which the new comment says reads the field "for every tool outside its legacy sets". For any `Tool(...)` that does not pass `tier=` explicitly and is not covered by those legacy sets — which was a valid registration before this change, since it defaulted to `"standard"` — `tools/tiers.py` now sees `""`, a value outside the documented set `core | standard | all`. If the lookup does not abort, the tool is placed at a nonexistent tier (silently wrong MCP exposure); if it does abort, a registration that previously worked now fails at import. Because this change is precisely about making command registration self-declaring across ~8 shared registry files, the failure mode is a new/forgotten command file that omits `tier`: the old contract let it work, the new one requires a validation path that is not present in the changed hunk, so the "a tool cannot land unplaced" guarantee is only a comment. Either add the enforcement (raise when `tier == ""` for a non-legacy tool) inside the registry change, or keep the safe default so omission fails predictably rather than landing in the tier table unplaced.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `tools=True` filter decides whether a family contributes MCP tools by searching the source text for the literal `\btool\s*=\s*"ddflow_`. A declaration that names its tool any other way — the pattern the change itself is meant to enable, "adding a command is one new file" — is skipped:
```
def _cmd(name, **kw): return Command(..., tool=f"ddflow_{name}", **kw)
COMMANDS = (_cmd("widget_status", ...),)
```
or `tool=_TOOL_STATUS` / `tool=TOOLS["widget"]`. `all_commands(tools=True)` then omits that family from `DECLARED`, and because the new guard only checks names already present in `LEGACY_ORDER`:
```
_unknown = [n for n in LEGACY_ORDER if n not in DECLARED and n not in HAND_WRITTEN]
```
a *new* tool (which by definition is not in `LEGACY_ORDER`) is dropped from `ORDER`/`TOOLS` with no error at all, while `all_commands()` (used by `exemptions.py`) still contains the command — the CLI command exists but the MCP tool silently disappears, which is exactly the divergence the declarative registration is supposed to remove. The same text heuristic in the opposite direction also lets a module be imported into the tool table on a mere docstring mention of `tool="ddflow_..."` when combined with a `COMMANDS =` line as described above.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py:21 (`_HAS_TOOL` / `family_modules(tools=True)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The probe `test_a_docstring_line_starting_with_commands_does_not_register_a_module` does not answer the original finding; it only exercises the "COMMANDS followed by a space" spelling. The same test proves the pattern still accepts a line that begins `COMMANDS:` (`assert _HAS_COMMANDS.search("COMMANDS: tuple[Command, ...] = (\n")`) and a line that begins `COMMANDS =` (`assert _HAS_COMMANDS.search("COMMANDS = ()\n")`), i.e. the discriminator is now the `:`/`=` after `COMMANDS`, not whether the line is inside a string. So registration is still decided by a text match and a helper module whose docstring contains a line such as

```python
"""Shared helpers for declared families.

COMMANDS: set this tuple in your module to register.
"""
```

still matches `_HAS_COMMANDS`, so `family_modules()` imports it and `all_commands()` dereferences its `COMMANDS` attribute (which does not exist, or is not a tuple of `Command`), raising at import/scan time exactly as described in the earlier review. The fix narrows the false-positive set from "any line starting with COMMANDS" to "any line starting with `COMMANDS:`/`COMMANDS =`", which is not the same as importing the module and checking the attribute has the expected type; the newly added assertions do not cover the colon/equals-in-a-string input, so the previous MEDIUM finding still holds.

chunk_findings.detail: The new comprehension reads `(tools[t] or {}).get("help_group")`. The `isinstance(tools, Mapping)` guard only checks the container type, never the value type, so any mapping whose values are not dict-like raises `AttributeError` on every help render. Before this change the values were never touched — `tools = list(tools)` simply took the keys — so a name-keyed registry such as `{"ddflow status": "show the queue", "ddflow claim": "claim the next item"}` (name → description string), or the name → `Command` shape the intent describes ("help group read from the Command itself", which would need `getattr`, not `.get`), used to render fine and now crashes with `'str' object has no attribute 'get'` / `'Command' object has no attribute 'get'`. Either guard the values (`isinstance(tools[t], Mapping)`) or read the attribute off the object that actually carries `help_group`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_HAS_COMMANDS = re.compile(r"^COMMANDS\s*(?::[^=\n]+)?=", re.MULTILINE)` only recognizes a *single-line* declaration: the optional annotation group is `[^=\n]+`, so any family whose annotation wraps is not imported at all. Concretely, a new one-file family written as

```python
COMMANDS: tuple[
    Command,
    ...,
] = (
    ...
)
```

fails the regex (after `COMMANDS:` the group can't cross the newline, the group is skipped, and `=` no longer follows), so `family_modules()` never imports the module and `all_commands()` silently omits all of its commands from `DECLARATIONS` in exemptions.py — the CLI commands simply do not exist, with no error, which defeats the "adding a command is one new file" contract (any formatting other than a one-line annotation silently unregisters the family). The same textual detector also over-matches: a helper module with a triple-quoted string containing a column-0 `COMMANDS = (` line is imported and then raises `AttributeError` on `m.COMMANDS`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py `_HAS_COMMANDS` (family_modules)

chunk_findings.detail: The MCP-table filter is purely textual and requires a literal double-quoted prefix: `_HAS_TOOL = re.compile(r'\btool\s*=\s*"ddflow_')`. A family that declares `tool='ddflow_x'` (single quotes), `tool=f"ddflow_{name}"`, or `tool=TOOL_X` where the name is a module constant, matches `_HAS_COMMANDS` but not `_HAS_TOOL`. In that case `all_commands(tools=True)` skips it, so the command keeps working on the CLI but is silently missing from the MCP tool table — a registration regression that produces no error and is only visible at call time. Because the filter decides correctness from source text rather than from the `Command` object itself, the two detectors can disagree about which families exist.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/__init__.py `_HAS_TOOL` (family_modules)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff changes `Tool.tier` from a working default (`"standard"`) to an empty-string sentinel and documents `""` as a "registration error", but nothing in the changed code enforces that. `tier` is not emitted by `tool_entry` either, so the only consumer is `tools/tiers.py`, which the new comment says reads the field "for every tool outside its legacy sets". For any `Tool(...)` that does not pass `tier=` explicitly and is not covered by those legacy sets — which was a valid registration before this change, since it defaulted to `"standard"` — `tools/tiers.py` now sees `""`, a value outside the documented set `core | standard | all`. If the lookup does not abort, the tool is placed at a nonexistent tier (silently wrong MCP exposure); if it does abort, a registration that previously worked now fails at import. Because this change is precisely about making command registration self-declaring across ~8 shared registry files, the failure mode is a new/forgotten command file that omits `tier`: the old contract let it work, the new one requires a validation path that is not present in the changed hunk, so the "a tool cannot land unplaced" guarantee is only a comment. Either add the enforcement (raise when `tier == ""` for a non-legacy tool) inside the registry change, or keep the safe default so omission fails predictably rather than landing in the tier table unplaced.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:573 (`Tool.tier` default)

chunk_findings.detail: Before this hunk, inclusion in `found` was decided purely by the textual match plus the import succeeding, so any family module whose `COMMANDS` was a non-`tuple` iterable was still registered and its commands were enumerated by `all_commands`. The new guard additionally requires the attribute to be exactly a `tuple`: given a family file `x.py` containing `COMMANDS = [Command(...)]` (or `COMMANDS = list(_build())`, or a generator), the text match `^COMMANDS\s*[:=]` succeeds and the module is imported, but `isinstance(..., tuple)` is `False`, so the module is dropped and every command in it silently disappears from `ddflow --help` and from the MCP tool table — no error is raised, and `tests/test_registration_by_convention.py` cannot catch it because both `all_commands()` and `DECLARED` go through this same `family_modules`, so the two sides stay equal. The comment says the check guards against "the text match can be fooled", but a fooled match (a `COMMANDS` line living inside a string/docstring, as in the new `zz_fake` test) never sets a module attribute at all, so `getattr(..., None) is None` already handles it; the `tuple` type restriction adds no protection and only rejects registrations that previously worked. Testing `is not None` (or `(tuple, list)`) would preserve the pre-existing contract.

chunk_findings.detail: The runner treats *any* non-None guard result as a refusal and short-circuits. The intent this change implements explicitly allows a guard to return a Note (`fn(ctx) -> Refusal(...) | Note | None`) and states that guidance/notes guards (P-lessons.delivery, B-lease-hold-visibility) and a suggestion guard (P-governor.tier-suggest) will be registered through this seam; the reviewed module provides no note path at all — `Check = Callable[[ClaimContext], "O.Outcome | None"]` and `first_refusal` returns `whatever is non-None`. Concretely: register a note guard at order 15 (the docstring says "Built-ins sit at orders 10, 20, 30; leave gaps", so 15 is the intended slot for such a guard) that returns a greeting/suggestion object. `first_refusal` returns that object immediately, so (a) `claim()` receives a note in the slot the docstring calls "the first refusal" and cannot distinguish it from a real refusal, wrongly refusing/reporting the claim, and (b) the checks at orders 20 and 30 (queued, reserved) — and any quota/limit refusal a later task registers — never run at all, so a claim that should have been refused (or merely annotated) is resolved by whichever guard happens to have something to say first. A guard-runner for this contract needs to accumulate notes while scanning the whole ordered list and return only the first actual refusal (and expose the notes), rather than `return`ing the first non-None value. The tests here do not cover it: every registered test guard returns either a refusal or `None` (`test_every_guard_passing_lets_the_claim_through`, `tests/test_claim_guards.py:52`), so the note case introduced by the very tasks this seam is being built for is untested.

chunk_findings.detail: `register` changed from `register(name: str, order: int = 50)` (order was the *first* positional parameter after `name`) to `register(name: str, fn: Check | None = None, order: int = 50)`, so a second positional argument is now bound to `fn` rather than `order`. Any registration that was legal at the parent commit, e.g. `register("quota-pause", 40)`, now silently calls `add(40)`: `(40).__doc__` resolves via the int type (no error at import), a `Guard` is stored whose `check` is the integer `40`, and the failure only surfaces later when the guard is invoked — `run` does `guard.check(ctx)` and raises `TypeError: 'int' object is not callable` at claim time. The change is not just internal: this module is the documented seam for the other guards named in the intent (B-quota-pause, RR-freshness, DX-sync-points, BR-phase-branch), each of which is expected to call `register` from its own module, and the docstring ("with no `fn`, a decorator") does not warn that positional `order` is no longer accepted. If the three built-in guards and any existing callers already use `order=`/`fn=` keyword form the bug is latent rather than live, but the signature change itself turns a previously-valid call into a silently misregistered guard instead of failing fast.
